why_angle: I could read one of the cited pages in full (StackandValue) and the start of a second (Dupple). Neither says what Windows does to a Bluetooth speaker that supports hands-free calling. TechRadar, Tom's Hardware, Tom's Guide and PC Gamer returned only their titles, and Wired blocked the fetch, so the angle agents could not rule them out. Microsoft's driver docs say that once any app opens the speaker's mic, playback switches to mono at 8 or 16 kHz, and on Windows 10 the stereo stream is thrown away. This page gives each candidate's Bluetooth profile or mic listing and its wired fallback, and picks the A2DP-only Creative Pebble Pro, which plays USB audio.

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Pebble Pro, PC port vs adapter: 30 W RMS ÷ 10 W RMS = 3× the rated output once a 30 W USB PD adapter powers it. Creative says the PD port "only provides power", so sound still has to come in over USB-C, Bluetooth or AUX. A 65 W charger such as the UGREEN Nexode 65W ($23.99 at UGREEN, 2026-11-08) covers the 30 W the Pebble Pro needs: {buy:ugreen-nexode-65w-3-port-charger}.
  • T60 vs Pebble Pro on a PC port alone: 30 W RMS ÷ 10 W RMS = 3×. The T60 runs from its own 18 V 2 A AC adapter, not the PC's USB port.
  • Pebble X Plus, PC port vs adapter: 30 W RMS ÷ 15 W RMS = 2×.
  • What hands-free mode costs: In Microsoft's own example, 48 kHz media plays into a call running at 16 kHz. That is 48 ÷ 16 = 3× fewer samples per second, and one channel instead of two. At narrowband 8 kHz it is 48 ÷ 8 = 6× fewer.
  • M60 bass limit: Erin's Audio Corner measured the M60 on a Klippel Near-Field Scanner. Spinorama.org's figures from that data put it 6 dB down at 62.3 Hz. Its preference score rises from 4.6 to 7.33 with an ideal subwoofer: 7.33 − 4.6 = 2.73 points. GadgetGuy measured the Z407's bass peaking at 64 Hz.

Why a Bluetooth speaker with a mic goes mono on a PC

Windows plays music to a Bluetooth speaker over A2DP, the stereo profile. On Windows 11, a speaker that also supports the Hands-Free Profile (HFP) gets a microphone input. Microsoft's driver documentation says Windows switches the speaker to HFP when any app opens that input or starts a playback stream in the Communications category. HFP is mono, at 8 kHz (narrowband, SBC) or 16 kHz (wideband, mSBC), and Windows resamples everything else that is playing to match. Windows 10 is worse: while the speaker is in hands-free mode, "any audio streaming to the stereo output is discarded."

There are three ways around it:

  • Buy a speaker with no hands-free profile. Creative lists only A2DP for the Pebble Pro and the Pebble X Plus. Microsoft says an A2DP-only device gets an output and no input, so call apps have to use the webcam, headset or desk mic, and the speakers keep playing in stereo.
  • Use the wired input. USB-C audio (Pebble Pro, Pebble X Plus, Pebble V3, T60, M60), micro-USB (Z407) or 3.5 mm skips Bluetooth profiles entirely.
  • Keep the speaker off the mic list. The Creative T60 lists HFP. Over Bluetooth, set Windows' default microphone and each call app's mic to another device, or play to the T60 over USB-C.

On a PC, the codec matters less than the profile. Microsoft's list of Windows codecs is aptX Adaptive (Windows 11 24H2, only on select Qualcomm radios), AAC (Windows 11 only), aptX Classic and SBC. LDAC is not on it. Edifier specifies the M60's LDAC for Android 8.0 or later, so from a Windows PC the M60 falls back to SBC. Every Creative model here lists SBC only. Bluetooth LE Audio came to Windows 11 in version 22H2. Microsoft says its LC3 codec has to come from the PC's audio driver or Bluetooth controller, so an LE Audio-ready speaker only gets LE Audio on PCs built for it.

Not recommended

The Marshall Emberton III as a PC speaker for calls. Marshall builds in a microphone for hands-free calling. That is exactly the setup Windows switches to mono 8 or 16 kHz when Teams or Discord opens a mic. Marshall lists no wired audio input (the USB-C cable is for charging), so there is no cable to fall back on. It suits a phone and a bag, not a desk PC that takes calls.
